summary: Serialize physical KVM actions across OS users, containers and target aliases, and stop burning single-use authorizations on lock-setup failures.
reason: The generated target lock keyed on os.UserCacheDir() and the raw target string. Two consequences: processes owned by different OS users (or in containers with separate cache dirs) took different lock files for one physical device, and two aliases for the same device ('kvm1' vs 'https://kvm1:443') also took different locks. Either case lets keyboard, mouse, switching and cleanup actions interleave on real hardware. Separately, ExecuteAuthorized consumed the single-use authorization before acquiring the lock, so any lock-setup failure destroyed the token for a workflow that never touched the device.
change: withTargetLock now derives its key from canonicalTargetIdentity(target), which normalizes scheme, case, default port and path so every alias of one endpoint maps to one lock. ExecuteAuthorized keys the lock on lockIdentity(device, target), which prefers the device's real endpoint (KVMDDevice.Endpoint reports the client's RequestBaseURL) over the free-form --target label, so unrelated labels aimed at one KVM still serialize. The lock lives in a single fixed shared directory (KVMCTL_LOCK_DIR, default /tmp/kvmctl-locks) rather than a privilege-dependent path, created world-writable with the sticky bit and validated (never chmod-ed) when pre-existing; lock files are opened 0666 with O_NOFOLLOW so a second OS user can contend on the same inode. ExecuteAuthorized acquires the device lock before consuming the token, re-checking context cancellation after the potentially blocking acquire. The Windows default is the machine-wide %ProgramData%\\kvmctl\\locks (falling back to %SystemRoot%\\Temp) rather than os.TempDir(), which honors TMP/TEMP and resolves to the per-user %LOCALAPPDATA%\\Temp for an interactive logon; defaultSharedLockDirFor takes goos and getenv so the Windows path is verified from any host instead of being skipped in CI.
verification: internal/sequence/crossuser_lock_test.go, atomic_consume_test.go and endpoint_lock_test.go. Every regression test was confirmed to FAIL against the code it guards: raw-label hashing reports 4 concurrent holders of the device lock; consume-before-lock loses the token on lock failure; keying on the --target label instead of the device endpoint reports 3 workflows driving one KVM concurrently. TestTokenConsumptionIsAtomicAcrossProcesses races 8 real OS processes against one token and asserts exactly one wins; with the store flock removed it reports 8/8 winners, confirming the existing flock (not a process-local mutex) is what makes consumption atomic - the review's third finding was therefore not valid. go build, go vet, go test ./..., go test -race ./internal/sequence/..., and cross-builds for windows/amd64, windows/arm64, linux/amd64, linux/arm64 and darwin/arm64 all pass. TestWindowsDefaultLockDirIsMachineWide simulates two interactive logons and was confirmed to FAIL against an os.TempDir()-style default (alice and bob receive different lock directories). Windows amd64/arm64 vet and cross-builds pass.
notes: Processes in separate mount namespaces still need KVMCTL_LOCK_DIR pointed at a shared bind mount; the kernel cannot serialize on distinct inodes. This is documented at the constant and surfaced as a loud error rather than silent non-serialization.
